one_liner: Header-only C++17 expression-template AD library; author reports 2-10x over Adept and 2-19x over Stan Math gradients.
what_it_does: Computes gradients of scalar functions by forward mode (ForwardVar<T>) or reverse mode (Var<T, scl|vec|mat>). It is not a drop-in replacement for an operator-overloading tape: you build an expression object, bind it to value/adjoint storage (ad::bind or bind_cache), call ad::autodiff(expr, seed), then read adjoints with get_adj(). Shared subexpressions go through 'placeholder' assignments (w = cos(v)) glued with operator,; control flow is expressed with ad::if_else, ad::for_each, ad::sum/prod over ranges.
how_it_is_fast: There is no runtime tape. The computation graph is a compile-time expression template (no virtual calls, no per-node heap allocation), and the exact value/adjoint storage size is computed up front so one contiguous block is allocated ('lazy allocation'). Vector/matrix variables store 'a pair of pointers to a matrix of doubles' instead of a matrix of (value, adjoint) pairs, so Eigen can emit packed SIMD (the paper shows vaddpd vs Stan's scalar vaddsd). C++17 if constexpr/SFINAE detects constant arguments and precomputes things like sufficient statistics in normal log-pdf.
when_to_use: Repeated gradient evaluation of a fixed-structure scalar objective (MCMC/HMC log-densities, MLE, regression likelihoods) where the graph is built once and re-evaluated with new inputs.
Vectorized objectives over Eigen vectors/matrices (sums, log-sum-exp, normal log-pdf), where the paper shows the largest gaps (about 9-19x vs Stan, 9-10x vs Adept).
Projects already using Eigen 3.3 and C++17 that want a small, MIT-licensed header-only AD dependency.
First-order gradients only, on x86-64 with -O3 -march=native.
when_not_to_use: Data-dependent dynamic graphs (graph shape changes per call, arbitrary loops/branches on runtime values): you must restate them with if_else/for_each, which a tape-based library (Adept, XAD, CppAD) handles naturally.
Higher-order derivatives, Jacobians of vector functions, sparse matrices or checkpointing: not supported (open issues #75, #101, #109, #28; the paper calls higher order 'a great challenge').
Workloads dominated by dense matrix products: the paper shows FastAD only comparable to Adept and about 2x over Stan there.
Production use needing a maintained library: last commit Sept 2023, and the paper says function/distribution/decomposition coverage is incomplete.
Builds with GCC 16 at -O3 until PR #111 lands (see gotchas).

integration.dependencies: Eigen 3.3 (GoogleTest and Google Benchmark for dev builds only)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; benchmarks used GCC 10; developed mainly with Clang; CMake package (FastAD::FastAD) or FetchContent of tag v3.2.1
integration.platforms: any platform Eigen supports; CI on Linux and macOS; benchmarked on x86-64 only
integration.thread_safety: not documented; expressions bind to mutable value/adjoint buffers, so treat each bound expression and its Vars as single-threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the arithmetic syntax resembles Adept/Stan, but code must be rewritten into bound expression objects with explicit placeholders and seeds

gotchas: Evaluating an expression that was never bound to storage segfaults (README warns explicitly); use ad::bind(...) unless you manage buffers yourself.
Adjoints accumulate: call reset_adj() on every Var, placeholders included, before differentiating again or gradients are wrong.

Open issue #110 (2026): with g++-16 at -O3, RcppFastAD examples segfault in memcpy or hit Eigen's 'DenseBase::resize() does not actually allow to resize' assertion; it goes away with -fno-inline or Clang. Unmerged PR #111 (Sept 2026) fixes Eigen::Map rebinding in ValueView::bind().
&& and || are undefined behavior on multi-dimensional non-boolean expressions; setting several forward-mode adjoints gives a scaled directional derivative.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FastAD over XAD when the objective is a fixed, Eigen-vectorized statistical model and you want the smallest header-only dependency. Pick XAD when you need a maintained, tape-based library that handles arbitrary C++ control flow, higher-order modes and checkpointing.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's unrefereed arXiv preprint (2102.03681), built with GCC 10, C++17, -O3 -march=native on an 8-core Google Cloud Xeon VM (model not stated), FastAD's gradient time beat Adept 2.0.8 and Stan Math 3.3.0 by about 10x/15x (sum), 2.5x/7.7x (log-sum-exp), 9x/19x (normal log-pdf), 10x/8.6x (Bayesian regression) and 2x/2.6x (stochastic volatility). Matrix product was roughly a tie with Adept. The harness is public (JamesYang007/ADBenchmark, tested only on macOS Catalina). The README's 'orders of magnitude' claim is not supported by these numbers.
status_note: Stale since Sept 2023 (one community PR open for a GCC 16 miscompile), but MIT-licensed and header-only, so it can be vendored; the R package RcppFastAD still depends on it.
